spots.name: Pioneer Square
spots.label: Pioneer Square

text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops close to this spot, so head for the Pioneer Square neighbourhood in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle. From there, the little triangular plaza is east, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: This is an open city street corner and public square, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any nearby attraction, such as the Smith Tower observation deck, which is paid.
text.geographic_location: Pioneer Square is in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle, a short way inland from the Elliott Bay waterfront.
text.description: Pioneer Square is a neighbourhood in the southwest corner of downtown Seattle, once the heart of the city, and it is named after a small triangular plaza near First Avenue and Yesler Way, once called Pioneer Place. Seattle's founders settled here in 1852. Most of the early wooden buildings burned in the Great Seattle Fire of 1889, and by the end of 1890 dozens of brick and stone buildings had replaced them. Those late 19th-century buildings, mostly in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, still give the neighbourhood its look, and the area is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a historic district. That mix of dark brick, old ironwork and street corners is what makes it good for phone photos. From here Smith Tower rises behind the parking garage known as the sinking ship. It is a good place for a wide, street-level shot with the whole scene in one frame, and it works especially well after rain, when puddles reflect the tower and buildings. If you want the classic view of the cast-iron pergola, with the totem pole and brick buildings around it, walk on to Pioneer Place Park. Occidental Park is the one for Smith Tower above the brick buildings. Keep an eye on your phone and your surroundings while you frame your shots.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If the reflection is the subject, tap on the puddle instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of James Street and Yesler Way (corner near the parking garage known as the sinking ship). Smith Tower rising behind the parking garage, with a wide-angle view that works especially well when puddles reflect the scene after rain. Stand on James Street and Yesler Way, at the corner near the parking garage known as the sinking ship. From here Smith Tower rises behind the garage. The small plaza and the pergola are a short walk to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so Smith Tower, the parking garage and the street all fit in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, calmer shot, or the telephoto if your phone has one (2x-5x) to pick out the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone level so the tall building does not lean. After rain, hold the phone low over a puddle so the tower and buildings reflect in it. For the classic pergola shot, walk on to Pioneer Place Park. Occidental Park is the one for Smith Tower above the brick buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just after rain, when puddles have formed, is the best time for the reflection shot. Golden hour suits the view of Smith Tower above the brick buildings in Occidental Park.

spots.name: Pike Place Market
spots.label: Pike Place Market

text.directions_text: From Downtown Seattle, the market is on the western side of the centre, by the waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The market is a working public market with streets and arcades that visitors walk through, but individual shops and stalls keep their own times, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Pike Place Market sits roughly in the north-west corner of Downtown Seattle's central business district, with Belltown to the north and the waterfront and Elliott Bay to the south-west. Its main street, Pike Place, runs north-west from Pike Street to Virginia Street.
text.description: Pike Place Market is a public market on the western edge of Downtown Seattle, looking out over Elliott Bay. It opened on 17 August 1907 and is one of the older continuously operated public farmers' markets in the United States. It is also Seattle's most popular tourist destination, with more than 20 million visitors a year. The classic photo here is the red neon Public Market Center sign and clock, shot head-on with the market entrance and street life behind it. Because the sign sits at the bottom of a slope, standing uphill gives a cleaner view than standing right under it. The market is built on the edge of a steep hill, with the covered arcades on the upper street level selling fish, fresh produce and crafts, and more shops on lower levels below. If you want a calmer view, try Pike Street for a street scene with Puget Sound behind it, or MarketFront for wide views over Elliott Bay and the Great Wheel. It gets very busy at the sign, so go early if you can, and keep an eye on the traffic.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the red neon keeps its colour instead of washing out. Take a few shots, as people and vehicles will keep moving through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of 1st Avenue and Pine Street (center of the crosswalk, uphill from the sign). The red neon Public Market Center sign and clock framed head-on, with the market entrance and street traffic behind. Use the uphill crosswalk near the Public Market Center sign. From here the red neon sign and clock face you directly, with the market entrance and street traffic behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the sign head-on. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or crowds stop you stepping back, or if you want more street and sky. Try 2x to pull the sign closer without walking into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the sign in the middle, with the clock level against a horizontal line. Include a little of the street and market entrance behind it to show where you are. For a different view, Pike Street gives a quieter street scene with Puget Sound behind, and MarketFront looks wide over Elliott Bay and the Great Wheel.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, because the crowds at the sign are heavy later in the day. Views of Mount Rainier and the Olympics from MarketFront depend on clear weather.

spots.name: Smith Tower
spots.label: Smith Tower

text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Pioneer Square, the neighbourhood around the tower. Occidental Square is a square within Pioneer Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: Occidental Square is an open public space, but the tower's observation deck is a paid attraction, so check the official site before you go if you want to go up.
text.geographic_location: Smith Tower is in the Pioneer Square neighbourhood of downtown Seattle, at the north-east corner of Yesler Way and Second Avenue. Occidental Square, where you take the photo, is a short walk to the south-west in the same neighbourhood.
text.description:
Smith Tower stands in the Pioneer Square neighbourhood and is one of the easiest Seattle buildings to pick out in a photo, thanks to its pyramid-shaped crown. It was completed in 1914 at 38 storeys and 462 ft (141 m), and at the time it was among the tallest skyscrapers outside New York City. It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until 1931, and the tallest on the US West Coast until the Space Needle overtook it in 1962. It is named after Lyman Cornelius Smith, the firearm and typewriter businessman who started the project, and it became a Seattle landmark in 1984.

The best photo here shows the whole tower in its setting, not just the building. That mix of old brick streets and a tall classical tower is what makes the shot work. Golden hour gives the warmest light. If you have time for a second angle, Yesler Way gives a wide view of the tower rising above a parking garage, with reflections in the wet pavement after rain.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's brightest face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the pale crown keeps its detail. Take a few shots, because people will walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Occidental Square. The tower's pyramid crown rising over the historic Pioneer Square streetscape, framed by the square's green space. The tower's pyramid crown rises over the Pioneer Square streetscape, with the square's green space as your foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the crown, the buildings and the green space of the square in one frame. If you want just the pyramid top, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone). Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for Yesler Way or when you walk closer to the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the crown in the top third. Use trees or the edge of the green space as a frame at the bottom or side, and keep your phone level so the tower's edges stay straight. For a different view, Yesler Way gives a wide-angle shot of the tower above a parking garage. After rain, the wet pavement adds reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low, warm light falls on the streetscape and the tower.
